segments.title: Opening and Matassa's three sons
segments.summary: Interviewer opens the session; Matassa gives his three sons' birth years and what they do.

segments.title: Meeting young Allen Toussaint and the Danny Kessler album
segments.summary: Matassa recalls Toussaint as a young session player picked out at an open call by Danny Kessler, who recorded him for RCA Victor.

segments.title: Independents versus majors in New Orleans recording
segments.summary: After early Columbia and Victor field work, postwar New Orleans recording came from independents, many arriving with no plan.

segments.title: Cheap studio rates and the ease of entering the record business
segments.summary: Sessions cost $15 an hour, later $35, and living was cheap, so many small labels put out a record or two.

segments.title: Distributors, label life cycles and the majors taking over
segments.summary: Independent distributors grew after the war; labels flashed and failed; the majors co-opted the business.

segments.title: Toussaint as arranger and producer, drawing out limited singers
segments.summary: Matassa praises Toussaint's ability to build arrangements around artists like Chris Kenner and describes how he worked in the studio.

segments.title: Dave Bartholomew as a taskmaster producer, and Lou Chudd
segments.summary: Bartholomew ran sessions like a sculptor and a bandleader; Lou Chudd valued his reliable output.

segments.title: Lou Chudd, advance pressings and disc jockey power
segments.summary: Chudd leaned on a few distributors and disc jockeys on what to release, sometimes against Bartholomew; the DJ scandals moved power to program directors.

segments.title: Joe Ruffino's ego and business practices
segments.summary: Ruffino is described as vain and ethically shaky, taking advantage of uninformed artists, with a lawsuit rooted in his practices.

segments.title: Ruffino, Morris Levy and the Carnival Time lawsuit
segments.summary: Discussion of Ruffino's lack of contracts and copyrights and Morris Levy as a gangster, with Ruffino living by the pen.

segments.title: Ruffino's habits, distributorship and stolen records
segments.summary: Ruffino would not sit with his back to the door, ran a distributorship, and reportedly received records stolen from Johnny Vincent's place.

segments.title: Ruffino's good records; Joe Banashak as a friend
segments.summary: Matassa credits Ruffino for recording good artists and introduces Banashak, whom he counted a friend despite human failings.

segments.title: Reel 2 begins; back to Banashak
segments.summary: Reel change; interviewer and Matassa sort out that they were on Banashak, not Ruffino.

segments.title: Minit Records and Art Rupe's hidden ownership of A1 Distributors
segments.summary: Minit was the most successful local label; Banashak was cheated when Art Rupe, who financed A1, would not let him buy him out.

segments.title: Banashak losing Allen Toussaint to Marshall Sehorn
segments.summary: While Toussaint was in service Banashak worked to keep him an artist, then Sehorn won him as partner, leaving Banashak feeling betrayed.

segments.title: Banashak's drinking, gambling and born-again faith
segments.summary: Banashak's life swung from drinking and gambling to born-again Christianity, with disillusionment, marital trouble and effects on A1.

segments.title: Lou Chudd's bottom-line dealings; Banashak above the rest
segments.summary: Matassa says Chudd invested only business relationships and underpaid Bartholomew; Banashak was more honest than anyone, majors included.

segments.title: Artists who squandered royalties and the lack of a New Orleans business infrastructure
segments.summary: Matassa recalls an artist given a $65,000 check who refused advice to buy a double house, and laments that many ended poor or bitter.

segments.title: Keeping family apart from the music scene; accusations of a studio clique
segments.summary: Matassa kept his family separate, spent long hours with musicians, and says he went out to find players rather than favor a clique.

segments.title: Dispute with Longhair's lawyer Zittler over song credits
segments.summary: Zittler challenges Matassa's writer credit on Professor Longhair songs such as Tipitina; Matassa is angry and waiting for a lawsuit.

segments.title: Al Young as Fats Domino's unsung producer and scout
segments.summary: Matassa credits Al Young with getting Fats Domino recorded, until Lou Chudd dropped him, and notes distributors doubled as talent scouts.

segments.title: Matassa's hedonistic years and not drinking
segments.summary: Matassa jokes about being a nondrinking Italian who enjoyed life and food, and had only one vice.

segments.title: The AFO musicians' cooperative and its bitterness
segments.summary: Matassa views the AFO of Harold Battiste and Red Tyler as a great idea that lost focus on blackness, and says they were cheated by a black man.

segments.title: Film work in New Orleans and King Creole
segments.summary: Matassa did sound work and consulting on films, thinks filmmakers treat music as an afterthought, and was a guest at the King Creole shoot.

segments.title: Fragment on New Orleans mayoral politics
segments.summary: Brief remark that a candidate blew his chances by not forming a biracial tandem.

segments.title: Reel 4 begins; Dover's pressing plant and Ralph Pate
segments.summary: Matassa explains Ralph Pate, who ran the pressing plant, and its capacity of about 15,000 records a day against 40-50,000 needed.

segments.title: Cash crunch, poor credit control and promotion spending errors
segments.summary: The company failed because Matassa extended credit carelessly and gave large promotion cash to people without monitoring.

segments.title: Bob Echols and misspent promotion money
segments.summary: Promoter Bob Robin (Robert Echols) was given a Cadillac and credit card and spent heavily on himself.

segments.title: Larry McKinley's half of a song and the Par-Lo mistake
segments.summary: Matassa talked a company into giving Larry McKinley half a song for promotion that did not pay off; he lost about $300,000.

segments.title: Funding everything with his own money and mortgages
segments.summary: Matassa had no partner or investor and mortgaged his properties to the hilt.

segments.title: NOLA artists, Barefoot and the Atlantic lawsuit
segments.summary: The Wardell Quezergue group on NOLA recorded Barefoot outside Atlantic's first refusal; Atlantic sued Matassa and won, taking over the record.

segments.title: White Cliffe label's weak artists and unpaid studio bills
segments.summary: Matassa let hopefuls use his studio and put out their records on White Cliffe, and NOLA left a $27,000 unpaid studio bill.

segments.title: Buying the Camp Street building and its four floors
segments.summary: Matassa bought a warehouse at 748 Camp Street; the floors held offices, studio, distribution storage and disk mastering.

segments.title: Consoles and tape machines at Camp Street
segments.summary: Description of the homemade rack modules, the later 16-input secondhand board and the eight-track machine.

segments.title: Control room design and monitor speakers
segments.summary: The control room layout, the argument over live versus dead rooms, and Matassa's Tannoy and Altec monitors.

segments.title: The isolated concrete studio floor
segments.summary: The studio floor was lightweight concrete on pads, with the drummer on a separate platform and baffles around.

segments.title: Drum miking, room reflections and the live studio sound
segments.summary: Matassa moves from one or two drum mics to five to seven, and explains the live room, late reflections and the dead rear.

segments.title: Recording with live audiences
segments.summary: Matassa recorded live albums and radio shows with audiences in the studio, which changes absorption and EQ.

segments.title: Changing recording technology: effects and dry tracks
segments.summary: Matassa lists plates, tape delay and springs, and describes bigger consoles and monitoring EQ while recording dry.

segments.title: Signing artists to White Cliffe for the wrong reasons
segments.summary: Matassa admits some signings were favors, and says that proved it by going broke.

segments.title: Running through White Cliffe releases
segments.summary: Interviewer lists White Cliffe artists such as Frankie Ford, Huey Piano Smith and Tommy Ridgley; Matassa gives short verdicts.

segments.title: Closing chatter about tape rewinds
segments.summary: Brief technical talk about cleaning tape with isopropyl alcohol.
